headline: Fort Trumbull Rip on the Ebb: Bunker Stacks Up, Bluefish Follow the Push
subhead: The new-moon surge finally dumped bait into the river mouth, and the bass and blues that had been picking at stragglers are starting to commit.
body_markdown:
The current seam off Fort Trumbull has been running harder than it has all summer, and that's the tell. When the ebb pulls that extra half-knot off the point and the bunker schools start balling up tight against it instead of scattering, you know the tide range is doing its job. That's exactly what's been happening the last several days as the new-moon surge worked through the river system — bigger swings, faster water, and bait getting squeezed into places predators can pin it. We flagged this coming — said the striper and bluefish activity would build at the river mouth as that tidal push tightened up the bunker schools — and this week it showed up right on schedule.

Water temps at the mouth are still sitting in the upper 60s, 69 and change on the outside readings, which is warm enough to keep everything active but not yet the number that pulls the blackfish out in force. That's still a couple weeks off — the rockpiles off Pleasure Beach and the riprap along the sub base fence line are starting to show a few tog feeling around, but the real push comes once that water eases down into the mid-60s. Right now the story is bass and blues working bait, and there's enough of it to make the trip worth planning around the tide rather than the clock.

The better bite has been on the last two hours of the ebb through Fort Trumbull and down toward the Ledge Light approach, where the river current collides with the harbor's outgoing flow and creates that seam of nervous water you can see from shore on a calm morning. Bass in the 24 to 32-inch class have been holding on the deep side of that seam, 15 to 20 feet down, and they're eating peanut bunker fished on a fish-finder rig or snagged live off the surface schools and drifted back into the current edge. Bucktails in white or bunker-pattern, 1 to 1.5 ounce, worked with a slow lift-and-drop through that same depth band have also been drawing strikes, especially in the last hour of light when the bait gets nervous and starts skipping.

Gold Star Bridge has been more of a mixed bag. The pilings on the downriver side, where the current wraps and slows just enough to hold bait in the shadow line, have given up blues to 4 and 5 pounds on the incoming tide, mostly on cast metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks worked fast through the wash. But it's been spotty, on-again-off-again with the tide stage rather than a steady grind, and a few boats have reported working the pilings for an hour with nothing before the blues show up in a five-minute window and then vanish. If you're fishing there, plan your session around the top of the incoming and be ready to move if it goes quiet — don't sit on dead water waiting for it to turn on.

Ocean Beach and the outer bar have had scattered blitz activity in the early morning, small stuff mostly — schoolie bass and cocktail blues chasing peanut bunker pushed out of the harbor on the ebb, visible from the seawall on a still morning. Nothing sustained yet, but that's consistent with what's building up and down the coast right now — the fall bunker migration is starting to tighten from the bigger bays down through southern New England, and the size class of bluefish showing up elsewhere in the region has been notably heavier than the summer average. That usually means the bigger blues aren't far behind the schoolies working New London's beaches, and when they show, the harbor mouth and the flats off Pleasure Beach are where they'll stage first.

Hickory shad have thinned out from where they were a few weeks back — the tail end of that run typically clears out through mid-September, and this year's been no different. A few stragglers are still showing on the flood tide up near the old rail bridge pilings, taking small shad darts and tiny Kastmasters, but that bite is closing fast. Porgies have held steady in the harbor on the deeper structure — 20 to 30 feet off the state pier and around the mooring fields — with sea worms and clam on standard porgy rigs still the most reliable producer, though the average size has been unremarkable, mostly 9 to 11 inches with the occasional keeper mixed in.

Looking at the next several days, the tide range is still building toward full strength off that new moon, which should keep pushing bait through the system and keep the bass and blues committed rather than just sampling. If the wind stays out of the northwest and holds the water clean through the week, Fort Trumbull on the last two hours of the ebb remains the highest-percentage window, with Gold Star's pilings a solid secondary play on the top of the flood. Once the tide range starts easing back after the full push, expect the bite to spread out a bit — less concentrated but more consistent through the day rather than confined to those tight windows. The blackfish pattern is still a couple weeks out, but with water temps trending down slowly, it's worth starting to scout the rockpiles now so you know where the bait's holding when that mid-60s number finally arrives.
